Notebook Role: Phase 5 – Modeling Scaffold¶

This is the core modeling notebook:

  • Loads Phase 3 artifacts (lexicon, hybrid, labels)
  • Encodes labels consistently
  • Provides an editable model cell for team hot‑swaps
  • Includes GridSearchCV tuning for linear models
  • Hardened evaluation functions (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC‑AUC, confusion matrix, classification report)
  • Runs Lexicon‑onPly and Hybrid tracks with 5‑fold CV
  • Compares Macro‑F1 scores visually

Purpose: train/test with 5‑fold CV — reproducible, audit‑ready evaluation pipeline for all team models.

Do not edit unless you need additional libraries.
This cell provides the common imports for all models and evaluations.

from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV

# Define your Linear SVM model wrapped with calibration
# LinearSVC is fast and scalable; calibration adds probabilities for ROC-AUC
base_model = LinearSVC(
    C=1.0,
    class_weight="balanced",
    random_state=42,
    max_iter=5000
)

model = CalibratedClassifierCV(
    estimator=base_model,  # use 'estimator' instead of 'base_estimator'
    cv=3  # calibration folds
)

print("Section 4: LinearSVC + CalibratedClassifierCV model defined successfully")
print(model)

Section 4a: Hyperparameter Tuning (Editable)¶

Do not edit.
This cell runs GridSearchCV on the model defined in Section 4, using f1_macro as the scoring metric.
It will search across a parameter grid appropriate for linear models (LogisticRegression, LinearSVC, RidgeClassifier, Perceptron).

In [ ]:
In [16]:
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, train_test_split # Added imports

# Subsample training data for faster grid search
X_sub, _, y_sub, _ = train_test_split(
    X_train_lex, y_train_enc,
    train_size=50000, stratify=y_train_enc,
    random_state=42
)

# Parameter grid for LinearSVC (calibration wraps it, so tune base model)
param_grids = {
    "LinearSVC": {
        "C": [0.1, 1, 10],
        "loss": ["hinge", "squared_hinge"]
    }
}

# Detect model type and select grid
model_name = "LinearSVC"
param_grid = param_grids.get(model_name, {})

if param_grid:
    grid = GridSearchCV(
        estimator=LinearSVC(class_weight="balanced", random_state=42, max_iter=5000),
        param_grid=param_grid,
        scoring="f1_macro",
        cv=2,          # fewer folds for speed
        n_jobs=-1,
        verbose=2
    )
    grid.fit(X_sub, y_sub)
    print(f"Best params for {model_name}:", grid.best_params_)
    print(f"Best CV Macro-F1 for {model_name}:", grid.best_score_)

    # Refit final calibrated model on full training set with best params
    tuned_base = LinearSVC(
        C=grid.best_params_["C"],
        loss=grid.best_params_["loss"],
        class_weight="balanced",
        random_state=42,
        max_iter=5000
    )
    model = CalibratedClassifierCV(
        estimator=tuned_base,  # <-- use 'estimator' here
        cv=3
    )
    model.fit(X_train_lex, y_train_enc)
    print("Final calibrated model retrained on full dataset with best params.")

else:
    print(f"No parameter grid defined for {model_name}. Please add one to param_grids.")

    plt.scatter(pca_results[mask, 0], pca_results[mask, 1], label=label, alpha=0.6, s=15)

plt.xlabel("Principal Component 1")
plt.ylabel("Principal Component 2")

def plot_confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred, classes):
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=True, fmt='d', cmap='Blues',
                xticklabels=classes, yticklabels=classes)
    plt.title('Confusion Matrix: SVM Sentiment Classification')
    plt.ylabel('Actual Sentiment')
    plt.xlabel('Predicted Sentiment')
    plt.show()

# Fix: Define y_pred and class_names
y_pred = model.predict(X_val_lex) # Make predictions on the validation set
class_names = le.classes_.tolist() # Get class names from the LabelEncoder

plot_confusion_matrix(y_val_enc, y_pred, class_names)

This bar chart compares Precision, Recall, and F1-Score across Negative, Neutral, and Positive classes to identify which sentiment is the hardest to predict.
In [19]:
from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_fscore_support

def plot_classification_metrics(y_true, y_pred, classes):
    precision, recall, f1, _ = precision_recall_fscore_support(y_true, y_pred)

    metrics_df = pd.DataFrame({
        'Class': classes,
        'Precision': precision,
        'Recall': recall,
        'F1-Score': f1
    }).melt(id_vars='Class', var_name='Metric', value_name='Score')

    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    sns.barplot(data=metrics_df, x='Class', y='Score', hue='Metric')
    plt.title('Performance Comparison by Sentiment Class')
    plt.ylim(0, 1.1)
    plt.legend(loc='lower right')
    plt.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)
    plt.show()

plot_classification_metrics(y_val_enc, y_pred, class_names)

#Multi-class ROC & Precision-Recall Curves
These curves are essential for understanding how the model handles the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity.
In [20]:
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, auc, precision_recall_curve, average_precision_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import label_binarize
from itertools import cycle

# Binarize the labels for multi-class plotting
y_val_bin = label_binarize(y_val_enc, classes=[0, 1, 2])
# Use predict_proba for CalibratedClassifierCV
y_score = model.predict_proba(X_val_lex)

# --- ROC Curve ---
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
colors = cycle(['red', 'gray', 'green'])
for i, color in zip(range(len(class_names)), colors):
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_val_bin[:, i], y_score[:, i])
    roc_auc = auc(fpr, tpr)
    plt.plot(fpr, tpr, color=color, lw=2, label=f'{class_names[i]} (AUC = {roc_auc:0.2f})')

plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], 'k--', lw=1)
plt.title('Multi-class ROC (One-vs-Rest)')
plt.xlabel('False Positive Rate')
plt.ylabel('True Positive Rate')
plt.legend(loc="lower right")
plt.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

# --- Precision-Recall Curve ---
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
for i, color in zip(range(len(class_names)), colors):
    precision, recall, _ = precision_recall_curve(y_val_bin[:, i], y_score[:, i])
    ap = average_precision_score(y_val_bin[:, i], y_score[:, i])
    plt.plot(recall, precision, color=color, lw=2, label=f'{class_names[i]} (AP = {ap:0.2f})')

plt.title('Multi-class Precision-Recall Curve')
plt.xlabel('Recall')
plt.ylabel('Precision')
plt.legend(loc="lower left")
plt.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

##SVM Decision Boundaries (PCA Space)
This graph visualizes how the SVM actually "cuts" the data space to separate classes. We use PCA to reduce the lexicon features to 2D so we can draw the boundary lines.
In [21]:
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.svm import SVC # Import SVC

# 1. Reduce features to 2D
pca = PCA(n_components=2)
X_val_2d = pca.fit_transform(X_val_lex[:1000]) # Use subset for speed
y_subset = y_val_enc[:1000]

# 2. Fit a temporary SVM on 2D data to visualize the boundaries
svm_2d = SVC(kernel='rbf', C=1.0).fit(X_val_2d, y_subset)

# 3. Create Meshgrid
h = .05
x_min, x_max = X_val_2d[:, 0].min() - 1, X_val_2d[:, 0].max() + 1
y_min, y_max = X_val_2d[:, 1].min() - 1, X_val_2d[:, 1].max() + 1
xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.arange(x_min, x_max, h), np.arange(y_min, y_max, h))

# 4. Predict over Meshgrid
Z = svm_2d.predict(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()])
Z = Z.reshape(xx.shape)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 7))
plt.contourf(xx, yy, Z, cmap='coolwarm', alpha=0.3)
scatter = plt.scatter(X_val_2d[:, 0], X_val_2d[:, 1], c=y_subset,
            cmap='coolwarm', edgecolors='k', alpha=0.6)
plt.title('SVM Decision Boundaries in 2D PCA Space')
plt.xlabel('PC1')
plt.ylabel('PC2')
plt.legend(handles=scatter.legend_elements()[0], labels=list(class_names))
plt.show()

##Radar Chart (Performance Spider Plot)
This plot is excellent for showing the "imbalance" in your model. It will show a large "web" for Positive and a tiny or non-existent one for Neutral.
In [24]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Data from your results
labels = np.array(['Precision', 'Recall', 'F1-Score'])
classes = ['Negative', 'Neutral', 'Positive']
# Scores from your classification report
stats = {
    'Negative': [0.503, 0.113, 0.184],
    'Neutral': [0.001, 0.001, 0.001], # Using near-zero for visualization
    'Positive': [0.830, 0.989, 0.902]
}

angles = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, len(labels), endpoint=False).tolist()
angles += angles[:1] # Close the circle

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8), subplot_kw=dict(polar=True))

for name, s in stats.items():
    s += s[:1]
    ax.plot(angles, s, linewidth=2, label=name)
    ax.fill(angles, s, alpha=0.25)

ax.set_theta_offset(np.pi / 2)
ax.set_theta_direction(-1)
ax.set_thetagrids(np.degrees(angles[:-1]), labels)
plt.title('Performance Comparison Across Sentiment Classes', size=15)
plt.legend(loc='upper right', bbox_to_anchor=(1.3, 1.1))
plt.show()

##Option 1: Built-in Class Weighting (Recommended)
This is the most efficient method for large datasets. It doesn't create new data; instead, it tells the SVM to "pay a higher price" (penalty) for misclassifying a Neutral or Negative sample than a Positive one.
In [ ]:
In [26]:
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer # Keep import for potential future use or context, but not in this specific pipeline
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, confusion_matrix
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# 1. Optimized Pipeline for Large-Scale Classification with already processed numerical features
# Since X_train_lex is already a numerical feature array, TfidfVectorizer is not needed.
pipeline = Pipeline([
    # Removed TfidfVectorizer as input X_train_lex is already numerical.
    ("svm", LinearSVC(
        class_weight="balanced",
        dual=False,
        max_iter=5000,
        C=0.1 # Stronger regularization to prevent overfitting to majority class
    ))
])

# 2. Train the Model
pipeline.fit(X_train_lex, y_train_enc)

# 3. Evaluate and Compare
y_pred = pipeline.predict(X_val_lex)
print("Improved Classification Report:")
print(classification_report(y_val_enc, y_pred, target_names=le.classes_))

# 4. Visualization: Improved Confusion Matrix
cm = confusion_matrix(y_val_enc, y_pred, normalize='true') # Normalize to see % accuracy per class
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.heatmap(cm, annot=True, fmt='.2%', cmap='Blues',
            xticklabels=le.classes_, yticklabels=le.classes_)
plt.title('Normalized Confusion Matrix (Balanced SVM)')
plt.ylabel('Actual Label')
plt.xlabel('Predicted Label')
plt.show()

import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Data for Class Distribution
def plot_class_distribution(y_train, y_val, target_names):
    train_counts = pd.Series(y_train).value_counts().sort_index()
    val_counts = pd.Series(y_val).value_counts().sort_index()

    df_dist = pd.DataFrame({
        'Class': target_names,
        'Training Set': train_counts.values,
        'Validation Set': val_counts.values
    }).melt(id_vars='Class', var_name='Dataset', value_name='Count')

    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    sns.barplot(data=df_dist, x='Class', y='Count', hue='Dataset', palette='muted')
    plt.yscale('log') # Using log scale because Validation set is massive (7.5M)
    plt.title("Class Distribution (Log Scale)")
    plt.ylabel("Number of Samples (Log)")
    plt.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)
    plt.show()

# Execute
plot_class_distribution(y_train_enc, y_val_enc, le.classes_)

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC
from sklearn.svm import SVC # Import SVC

def plot_svm_boundary(X, y, model, target_names):
    # Subsample for speed (essential for 7.5M rows)
    sample_size = 1000
    idx = np.random.choice(len(y), sample_size, replace=False)

    # Fix: Convert coo_matrix to csr_matrix before indexing for efficient row access
    if hasattr(X, "toarray") and not isinstance(X, np.ndarray):
        X_reduced = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(X.tocsr()[idx].toarray())
    else:
        X_reduced = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(X[idx])

    y_reduced = y[idx]

    # Create a mesh grid
    h = .02
    x_min, x_max = X_reduced[:, 0].min() - 1, X_reduced[:, 0].max() + 1
    y_min, y_max = X_reduced[:, 1].min() - 1, X_reduced[:, 1].max() + 1
    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.arange(x_min, x_max, h), np.arange(y_min, y_max, h))

    # Train a "proxy" SVM on the 2D data to show the boundary logic
    proxy_svm = LinearSVC(C=0.1, class_weight='balanced').fit(X_reduced, y_reduced)
    Z = proxy_svm.predict(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()])
    Z = Z.reshape(xx.shape)

    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 8))
    plt.contourf(xx, yy, Z, cmap=plt.cm.Paired, alpha=0.3)

    # Scatter plot of actual points
    scatter = plt.scatter(X_reduced[:, 0], X_reduced[:, 1], c=y_reduced,
                          edgecolors='k', cmap=plt.cm.Paired, s=30)

    plt.title("SVM Decision Boundaries (PCA-Reduced Space)")
    plt.xlabel("Principal Component 1")
    plt.ylabel("Principal Component 2")

    # Create Legend
    handles, _ = scatter.legend_elements()
    plt.legend(handles, target_names, loc="upper right")
    plt.show()

# Run this (will take ~1-2 minutes)
plot_svm_boundary(X_val_hybrid, y_val_enc, pipeline, le.classes_)

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer # Keep import for context, but not in pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report
from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE
from imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline as ImbPipeline
from sklearn.svm import SVC # Import SVC for visualization proxy

# 1. THE PIPELINE: SMOTE + FAST LINEAR MODEL
# We use SGDClassifier because standard SVC is too slow for 505k samples.
# Hinge loss makes it behave like a Linear SVM.
# Removed TfidfVectorizer as X_train_lex is already numerical.
model_pipeline = ImbPipeline([
    ("smote", SMOTE(random_state=42)), # Synthetically balances your classes
    ("svm", SGDClassifier(loss='hinge', random_state=42))
])

# 2. TRAIN
# Use X_train_lex and y_train_enc as these are defined from previous cells
model_pipeline.fit(X_train_lex, y_train_enc)
y_pred = model_pipeline.predict(X_val_lex)

# ==========================================================
# PLOT 1: PERFORMANCE COMPARISON (POSITIVE vs NEGATIVE vs NEUTRAL)
# ==========================================================
# Use y_val_enc and y_pred, and provide target_names for classification_report
report = classification_report(y_val_enc, y_pred, output_dict=True, target_names=le.classes_)
df_metrics = pd.DataFrame(report).transpose().iloc[:3, :3] # Keep only class metrics

df_metrics.plot(kind='bar', figsize=(10, 6), color=['#3498db', '#e67e22', '#2ecc71'])
plt.title('Sentiment Class Comparison after SMOTE')
plt.ylabel('Score')
plt.xlabel('Sentiment Class')
plt.xticks(rotation=0)
plt.legend(loc='lower right')
plt.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)
plt.show()

# ==========================================================
# PLOT 2: DECISION BOUNDARY (PCA PROJECTION)
# ==========================================================
# We sample 2000 points for visualization to keep the plot readable
# Use X_val_lex and y_val_enc
X_vis = X_val_lex[:2000]
y_vis = y_val_enc[:2000]

# Since TF-IDF is removed from the pipeline, directly apply PCA on numerical features
pca = PCA(n_components=2)
X_pca = pca.fit_transform(X_vis)

# Create a mesh grid for the boundary
h = .02
x_min, x_max = X_pca[:, 0].min() - 0.1, X_pca[:, 0].max() + 0.1
y_min, y_max = X_pca[:, 1].min() - 0.1, X_pca[:, 1].max() + 0.1
xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.arange(x_min, x_max, h), np.arange(y_min, y_max, h))

# Predict across the grid
# Train a small proxy SVM model on the 2D PCA points
proxy_svm = SVC(kernel='linear', C=1.0)
proxy_svm.fit(X_pca, y_vis)
Z = proxy_svm.predict(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()])
Z = Z.reshape(xx.shape)

# No need to convert string labels to numbers, y_vis is already numeric encoded
# Use le.classes_ for legend labels
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 7))
plt.contourf(xx, yy, Z, alpha=0.3, cmap='Set2')
sns.scatterplot(x=X_pca[:, 0], y=X_pca[:, 1], hue=le.inverse_transform(y_vis), palette='Set2', edgecolor='w', s=60)
plt.title('SVM Decision Boundary (SMOTE Balanced)')
plt.xlabel('Principal Component 1')
plt.ylabel('Principal Component 2')
plt.legend(title='Sentiment')
plt.show()

##Option3: Balanced Random Forest Method
This method works by "undersampling" the Positive majority class in every individual tree it builds, ensuring that each part of the model sees an equal number of Neutral and Positive samples.

        n_estimators=100,

        bootstrap=True,
        random_state=42,
        n_jobs=-1
    ))
])

##Option 4 :Improved Method: SGDClassifier with Hinge Loss
This method mimics a Linear SVM but uses an iterative optimization process that is significantly faster and more robust against class imbalance.
In [34]:
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDClassifier
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, confusion_matrix
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# 1. High-Performance Pipeline
# We use 'hinge' loss to make the SGD act like a Linear SVM
# We increase 'alpha' slightly to help with the heavy overlap seen in your PCA
# NOTE: TfidfVectorizer is for raw text. Since X_train_lex is numerical, we should skip TFIDF for now.
# If you were working with raw text data directly, this TFIDF step would be appropriate.
improved_pipeline = Pipeline([
    # Removed TfidfVectorizer as input X_train_lex is already numerical features.
    ("sgd", SGDClassifier(
        loss='hinge',           # Mimics SVM behavior
        class_weight='balanced', # Crucial to fix the 0% Neutral Recall
        penalty='l2',           # Prevents overfitting
        alpha=0.0001,           # Regularization strength
        max_iter=1000,
        tol=1e-3,
        random_state=42,
        n_jobs=-1               # Uses all CPU cores for speed
    ))
])

# 2. Fast Training
print("Training SGD Classifier on 505k samples...")
improved_pipeline.fit(X_train_lex, y_train_enc)

# 3. Evaluation
y_pred_new = improved_pipeline.predict(X_val_lex)
print("\nUpdated Classification Report:")
print(classification_report(y_val_enc, y_pred_new, target_names=le.classes_))

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

def plot_sentiment_metrics(y_true, y_pred, target_names):
    # 1. Extract the report as a dictionary
    report = classification_report(y_true, y_pred, target_names=target_names, output_dict=True)

    # 2. Format data for plotting
    data = []
    for sentiment in target_names:
        for metric in ['precision', 'recall', 'f1-score']:
            data.append({
                'Class': sentiment,
                'Metric': metric.capitalize(),
                'Score': report[sentiment][metric]
            })

    df_metrics = pd.DataFrame(data)

    # 3. Create the Plot
    plt.figure(figsize=(12, 7))
    sns.set_context("talk")
    ax = sns.barplot(x='Class', y='Score', hue='Metric', data=df_metrics, palette='magma')

    # Add Overall Accuracy Line
    plt.axhline(report['accuracy'], color='blue', linestyle='--', label=f"Overall Accuracy ({report['accuracy']:.2f})")

    # Add Macro F1 Line (True performance measure)
    plt.axhline(report['macro avg']['f1-score'], color='red', linestyle='-.', label=f"Macro F1 Avg ({report['macro avg']['f1-score']:.2f})")

    plt.title('Sentiment Class Comparison: SGD (SVM-Hinge) Performance', fontsize=16)
    plt.ylim(0, 1.1)
    plt.ylabel('Metric Score')
    plt.legend(bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1), loc='upper left')

    # Annotate bars with values
    for p in ax.patches:
        ax.annotate(format(p.get_height(), '.2f'),
                    (p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2., p.get_height()),
                    ha = 'center', va = 'center',
                    xytext = (0, 9),
                    textcoords = 'offset points',
                    fontsize=12)
    plt.show()

# Execute
plot_sentiment_metrics(y_val_enc, y_pred_new, le.classes_)

##Hybrid Sampling Strategy
Standard SMOTE can sometimes create "noisy" synthetic data if classes overlap. We will combine Random Under-sampling (to reduce the dominance of the Positive class) with SMOTE (to clarify the Neutral zone).
In [41]:
from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE
from imblearn.under_sampling import RandomUnderSampler
from imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline as ImbPipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDClassifier
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer # Keep import for context, but not in this specific pipeline

# 1. Define specific ratios to force model attention using integer labels
# 0: negative, 1: neutral, 2: positive (based on le.classes_)
# Current counts: positive=235384, negative=124820, neutral=49373

# Undersample the 'positive' class (label 2) to a target of, e.g., 150,000
under = RandomUnderSampler(sampling_strategy={2: 150000}, random_state=42)

# Oversample 'neutral' (label 1) and 'negative' (label 0) to, e.g., 200,000 each
over = SMOTE(sampling_strategy={1: 200000, 0: 200000}, random_state=42)

# 2. Optimized Pipeline
improved_svm = ImbPipeline([
    # Removed TfidfVectorizer as input X_train_lex is already numerical.
    ("under", under),
    ("over", over),
    ("sgd", SGDClassifier(loss='modified_huber', class_weight='balanced', random_state=42)) # 'modified_huber' allows probability tuning
])

improved_svm.fit(X_train_lex, y_train_enc)

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# 1. Get counts for Actual and Predicted
# We use the encoder or original labels to ensure alignment
unique_labels = ['Negative', 'Neutral', 'Positive']
actual_counts = pd.Series(y_val_enc).value_counts().sort_index().values

# Fix: Ensure pred_counts has an entry for all unique labels, even if 0
all_class_indices = np.arange(len(unique_labels)) # This creates [0, 1, 2]
pred_counts_series = pd.Series(y_pred).value_counts().reindex(all_class_indices, fill_value=0).sort_index()
pred_counts = pred_counts_series.values

# 2. Setup the Plot
x = np.arange(len(unique_labels))  # label locations
width = 0.35  # width of the bars

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
rects1 = ax.bar(x - width/2, actual_counts, width, label='Actual (Unseen Data)', color='#3498db')
rects2 = ax.bar(x + width/2, pred_counts, width, label='Predicted (Model)', color='#e67e22')

# 3. Add labels and formatting
ax.set_ylabel('Number of Samples')
ax.set_title('Comparison of Actual vs. Predicted Sentiment Distributions')
ax.set_xticks(x)
ax.set_xticklabels(unique_labels)
ax.legend()

# Add value labels on top of bars
ax.bar_label(rects1, padding=3)
ax.bar_label(rects2, padding=3)

fig.tight_layout()

# 4. Save to Colab Files
plt.savefig('Sentiment_Frequency_Comparison.png', dpi=300)
plt.show()

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pandas.plotting import parallel_coordinates
import numpy as np

# 1. SETUP FOR COLAB/JUPYTER
%matplotlib inline

def plot_sentiment_parallel_coordinates(df_val, feature_cols, target_col):
    """
    df_val: Your validation dataframe containing lexicon scores
    feature_cols: List of columns like ['vader_score', 'afinn_score', 'text_length']
    target_col: The column with labels [0, 1, 2] or ['Neutral', 'Negative', 'Positive']
    """

    # 2. STRATEGIC SAMPLING
    # We take 100 samples per class to avoid "Spaghetti" overlap
    # This ensures Neutral (your 0.11 recall class) is clearly visible
    sample_df = df_val.groupby(target_col).apply(lambda x: x.sample(min(len(x), 100))).reset_index(drop=True)

    # 3. NORMALIZATION (Crucial for Parallel Plots)
    # Scales all features to 0-1 so they fit on the same Y-axis
    plot_df = sample_df[feature_cols + [target_col]].copy()
    for col in feature_cols:
        plot_df[col] = (plot_df[col] - plot_df[col].min()) / (plot_df[col].max() - plot_df[col].min())

    # 4. PLOTTING
    plt.figure(figsize=(15, 8))

    # Custom Palette: Purple (Neutral), Blue (Negative), Gold (Positive)
    # Matches the 'viridis' style of your bar chart
    colors = ['#440154', '#31688e', '#fde725']

    parallel_coordinates(plot_df, target_col, color=colors, alpha=0.3, linewidth=2)

    # 5. STYLING
    plt.title('SVM Feature Pathways: Distinguishing Neutral Sentiment', fontsize=16, fontweight='bold')
    plt.ylabel('Normalized Feature Value (0 to 1)', fontweight='bold')
    plt.xlabel('Lexicon & Text Features', fontweight='bold')
    plt.legend(title='Sentiment Class', bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1), loc='upper left')
    plt.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

# --- EXECUTION ---
# Replace 'vader', 'afinn', 'len' with your actual column names
# features = ['vader_compound', 'afinn_score', 'text_length', 'tfidf_sum']
# plot_sentiment_parallel_coordinates(df_val, features, 'sentiment_label')

# 1. Prepare the Expanded Data

    'Method': ['CSV Linear', 'CSV_COST', 'SMOTE', 'SGD', 'Hybrid (SMOTE+SGD)', 'Random Forest', 'Neural Network'],
    'Neutral_Recall': [0.00, 0.00, 0.04, 0.00, 0.11, 0.15, 0.19],

}

df = pd.DataFrame(comparison_data)

# 2. Reshape for Seaborn (Melt)

        ax.annotate(format(height, '.2f'),
                    (p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2., height),
                    ha='center', va='bottom',
                    xytext=(0, 5),
                    textcoords='offset points',
                    fontsize=9, fontweight='bold')

# --- FIX 3: PREVENT CLIPPING ---
plt.tight_layout() # Ensures labels and legend fit in the final HTML export
plt.show()

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Data from your summary
labels = ['Neutral Recall', 'Negative F1', 'Macro Avg F1']
baseline = [0.00, 0.18, 0.36]
hybrid_final = [0.11, 0.36, 0.42]

x = np.arange(len(labels))
width = 0.35

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
rects1 = ax.bar(x - width/2, baseline, width, label='Baseline (CSV Linear)', color='#ff9999')
rects2 = ax.bar(x + width/2, hybrid_final, width, label='Final (Hybrid SMOTE+SGD)', color='#66b3ff')

ax.set_ylabel('Scores')
ax.set_title('The Performance Gap: Baseline vs. Optimized Final Model')
ax.set_xticks(x)
ax.set_xticklabels(labels)
ax.legend()

# Add improvement percentage labels
for i in range(len(labels)):
    improvement = ((hybrid_final[i] - baseline[i]) / (baseline[i] if baseline[i] != 0 else 1)) * 100
    ax.annotate(f'+{improvement:.0f}%',
                xy=(x[i] + width/2, hybrid_final[i]),
                xytext=(0, 3), textcoords="offset points",
                ha='center', fontweight='bold', color='darkblue')

plt.ylim(0, 0.55)
plt.show()
